title: GRASP: Graph Reasoning via Agentic Solving and Probing
one_liner: Let LLMs actively explore graph structure one neighbor at a time instead of trying to understand the whole graph at once.
lead: Large language models are good at language but struggle when you ask them to reason about graphs (networks of connected things, like social networks or road maps). When you dump an entire graph into the model at once, it forgets parts, miscalculates, and invents fake connections. GRASP solves this by letting the model actively ask for neighbors step-by-step, verify calculations with code, and gradually learn what the graph really looks like.

paras: Picture this: find the shortest path between two cities in a road network with a thousand cities and ten thousand roads. If someone hands you the entire list of roads in one block of text, three problems hit immediately: First, the list is too long to fit in your working memory at once — you can only keep maybe a few dozen roads in mind. Second, if you try to do arithmetic on the distances (add them up, compare them), mistakes creep in because there is too much to track. Third, your brain will invent plausible-sounding roads that were never in the list, just filling gaps because the picture is incomplete.

Large language models have the same three bottlenecks: limited context windows (can only hold so much text), unreliable arithmetic when juggling many numbers at once, and a tendency to hallucinate — invent connections and nodes that fit the pattern but were never in the original graph. A beginner's approach is just to paste the whole graph into the model and hope for the right answer. That predictably fails.

callout.html: Instead of ingesting the whole graph at once, let the model ask for one node's neighbors when it needs them, then use code to calculate answers reliably.

steps.text: Find the shortest path from A to E in this graph.
I am at A. What are my neighbors? System returns: B (distance 2.3), D (distance 1.8).
Model asks Python to compare 2.3 and 1.8, decide which is shorter, track cumulative distance.
D looks closer. What are D's neighbors? System: E (distance 1.1), B (distance 0.9).
After many such problems, model internalizes which types of graphs it saw and builds genuine intuition for navigation.

paras: GRASP changes how the model retrieves graph information: instead of reading the whole graph at the start, the model dynamically fetches neighbors on-demand as it explores. This turns a static, memorization problem into an active navigation task.

hidden.h2: Topological awareness: does the model truly understand the graph shape?
hidden.name: Genuine structure learning
paras: The real insight is whether the model is genuinely learning the structure or just memorizing paths it has seen. In early training, the model can still see the whole graph laid out, so it might just copy memorized solutions. But GRASP includes a later training phase where the graph structure is hidden from view — the model only gets results when it asks. At this point, if the model succeeds, it means the model has internalized the actual graph topology (how nodes connect), not just recalled a memorized answer.

The paper measures this by comparing performance in two training environments: one where the model can peek at the full graph structure, and one where it cannot. A large performance drop in the structure-blind phase reveals the model was mostly memorizing; stable performance shows it truly learned the shape.

heat.caption: Darker means better performance on structure-blind tasks; shows genuine learning, not memorization.

reads.html: The model is truly learning the graph shape if it navigates well even when it cannot see the full structure upfront.
GRASP uses staged RL: early phases expose full structure (learning-friendly), later phases hide it (verifying genuine topology internalization).

mechanism.h2: Why this works: active exploration plus verification
paras: The mechanism has three moving parts. First, on-demand neighbor retrieval shrinks the working memory problem: instead of holding a thousand nodes, the model keeps only the current node and its immediate neighbors in focus. It asks for neighbors when it needs them, like looking up one entry in a phone book rather than memorizing the whole directory.

Second, code interpretation removes arithmetic errors. When the model needs to compare distances or count steps, it hands the numbers to a Python interpreter which calculates perfectly. The model no longer has to guess whether 2.3 + 1.4 is 3.7 or make arithmetic errors under pressure.

Third, staged reinforcement learning forces genuine learning. In early training, the structure is visible (the model can cheat by memorizing). In later training, the structure is hidden and only revealed through queries. If the model succeeds in the hidden phase, it must have learned a real mental model of the graph — not just copied an answer. This selective pressure teaches the model to build and refine its internal understanding of how the graph is organized.

stages.s: Model asks for current node's neighbors
Code interpreter compares distances, tracks path
Model picks best next node to explore
Repeat until goal reached or time out
Final path cost; model's learned structure intuition

math.words: Staged loss equals: task reward minus a penalty term scaled by how far the model's current policy diverges from its previous safe policy, with the strength of that penalty decreasing over training stages.
symbols: reward for answering the question correctly
strength of the divergence penalty (decreases over stages)
how different the new policy is from the old one
model's current decision distribution (how it chooses neighbors)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the model answers a shortest-path question correctly: R_task = 10 points.
The new exploration policy is slightly different from the old one: KL divergence = 0.5.
Beta (penalty strength) is set to 2.0 in this training stage.
If the policy diverged a lot (KL = 2.0): Loss = 10 - 2.0 * 2.0 = 6.0 (worse, penalized).
As training progresses, beta shrinks (say to 0.1), so divergence is allowed: Loss = 10 - 0.1 * 2.0 = 9.8.
Early stages keep policy close to safe (high beta); later stages encourage exploration (low beta).

math.note: The staged reduction of beta is key: start conservative (learn from visible structure), then loosen up (explore blindly and discover genuine understanding).

charts.title: Passive ingestion (old way)
charts.note: Falls apart when graphs are large or completely different from training.

charts.title: GRASP with agentic exploration
charts.note: Stays stable and generalizes because staged training forces real learning of structure, not memorization; achieves 53% average boost on multi-domain benchmarks.

items.html: If the exploration sequence is too long, the model may lose track of which nodes it has already visited or what the current cumulative distance is, because the model's context window is finite. Shorter lookahead helps by reducing how far ahead the model must plan; explicitly storing visited nodes in memory reduces confusion about what was explored.
Querying neighbors one-by-one is slower than reading the whole graph once. On million-node graphs, thousands of queries add up. Batching queries or caching frequently-visited nodes is a mitigation.

items.b: Model overfits to training graph structure.
items.html: If the model only sees graphs of one specific type (e.g., road networks), it may not transfer to a different type (e.g., social networks). The paper tests this with unseen tasks; it passes, suggesting real generalization.
Pairing on-demand retrieval with code verification and staged training discipline forces the model to build and refine a genuine mental model of the graph topology.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple graph with 20-50 nodes and a handful of known shortest paths. Run the model in two modes: (1) full visibility (the model can see all edges upfront), and (2) query-only (the model must ask for neighbors). Measure the path cost and number of errors in each mode. The key result: performance should be nearly the same in both modes. If mode-2 (query-only) is much worse, the model was memorizing structure from mode-1, not learning it genuinely.
demo.closing: A small gap proves the model is learning real graph structure, not cheating.
